name: Éton (Edingding)
autonymMeaning: name of a tree; for the neighbours, the name of a great warrior
overview: The Edingding (Mengara), one of the great Éton lineages of the Lékié, neighbour the Medoum, Batchenga, Mvele and Mvog-Beloa. Coming from the other bank of the Sanaga via Emana, Talla, Saa and Elig-Fomo, they acquired their lands through friendship. An egalitarian and hospitable society, they grow cocoa and dance the bikutsi.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Group integrated with its neighbours (Medoum, Batchenga, Mvele, Mvog-Beloa); the Mengara come third in number, after the Essele and the Mvokani.
All speak Eton, despite variations in vocabulary and tones; it is also spoken at Saa, Elig-Fomo, Okola and Mugna.
To avoid incest, one takes one's spouse from outside the group; one may marry a “nephew” with no real kinship tie.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The Mengara obtained their lands thanks to the friendship of another group, a friendship founded on the Christian faith.
Having come from the other bank of the Sanaga, they passed through Emana, Nkengue, Elig-Fomo, Talla, Saa and Ondodo'o, and remain united with these places.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: An association-type organisation, where everyone is the equal of everyone else.
The chief never decides alone: he gathers his notables and the decision is then passed on; families also settle their affairs in council.
Anyone may speak in the assembly, in strict respect of the elders.
Formerly, elderly women prepared the girls for marriage, fathers educated the boys, and young women enlivened the celebrations with their cries of joy.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship, or matrilineal when the father is unknown; the wife joins her husband.
The boy becomes a man at around 20 by building his house and marrying; the girl becomes a woman by presenting her fiancé to her parents.
Steps: meeting, “knocking at the door”, handing over of the list, bride price; the bride price may follow the civil marriage.
Bride price: palm wine and kola (love), rum, goat; after the goat meal, people wipe their hands on their feet and pronounce blessings on the young woman.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: No ancestor worship.
Ngoag Ikula, “the bent rock”, at Minkama, is the place where unmarried men and women over 50 perform rites for the good of the group.
Birth is a reincarnation; death is natural. The dead are honoured during ceremonies, commemorations and prayers at the graves.
Incest is forbidden; certain game is forbidden to children and pregnant women.
Desecrating a grave led to the traditional prison; to wipe out a serious offence, a live goat was split open.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Cocoa is the men's main activity; maize, groundnut, cassava, tomato and sesame are also grown.
The land falls under the State unless there is a land title; seller and buyer go to the chief to lift customary rights.
Ancestral forge: crowbars, hoes, baskets, trays, drying racks and traditional beds.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Formerly a wrapper with a hat or obom for men, a loincloth of banana leaves for women; today, suits and kabas.
Modern medicine dominates; tradition is used mainly for blessings.
Beauty: cleanliness, strength, hard work; the well-groomed, hard-working woman, a good cook, with natural hair.
Courtship: the man offers presents, the woman cooks and gives the best to the man she loves.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: mendjan (balafons), bikutsi (“let us strike the ground”, sung and danced by women), minkul; ma'a drum.
Dances: bikutsi and mendjan at weddings, essani at the mourning of a respected elder, kam (“to tremble”) in joy.
A festival in honour of the great warrior was held every early January.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The group is known for its hospitality and solidarity, which bring it close to the Ewondo and the Bamiléké.

sections.title: The names
items: No masculine or feminine marker; names honour family members (in-laws, parents).
One does not change name; if a name brings bad luck, it is no longer given.
One calls indifferently by the real name, the pseudonym or the nickname.
Each family has its ancestor: that of the Mvog-Andela is called Nkomo.

lessons.title: Who are the Éton (Edingding)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Éton (Edingding) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Éton (Edingding) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Éton (Edingding) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Éton (Edingding) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Éton (Edingding) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Éton (Edingding) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Group integrated with its neighbours (Medoum, Batchenga, Mvele, Mvog-Beloa); the Mengara come third in number, after the Essele and the Mvokani. • All speak Eton, despite variations in vocabulary and tones; it is also spoken at Saa, Elig-Fomo, Okola and Mugna. • To avoid incest, one takes a spouse from outside the group; one may marry a “nephew” with no real kinship tie. • The Mengara obtained their lands thanks to the friendship of another group, a friendship founded on the Christian faith. • Coming from the other bank of the Sanaga, they passed through Emana, Nkengue, Elig-Fomo, Talla, Saa and Ondodo'o, and remain attached to these places.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Edingding (Mengara), one of the great Éton lineages of the Lékié, neighbour the Medoum, Batchenga, Mvele and Mvog-Beloa. Coming from the other bank of the Sanaga via Emana, Talla, Saa and Elig-Fomo, they acquired their lands through friendship. An egalitarian and hospitable society, they grow cocoa and dance the bikutsi.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Éton (Edingding) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Éton (Edingding)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Éton (Edingding), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Éton (Edingding).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Éton (Edingding), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Éton (Edingding).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: cassava leaves, okok, gnara, groundnut dishes, cassava and sweet potato. • Drinks: palm wine, odontol, mbatoro (spirits). • Cocoa is the men's main activity; maize, groundnuts, cassava, tomatoes and sesame are also grown.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Éton (Edingding) eat mainly cassava leaves, okok, gnara, groundnut dishes. Traditional drinks: palm wine, odontol, mbatoro. These foods are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Éton (Edingding): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)

steps.instruction: Among the Éton (Edingding), traditional dances (bikutsi, essani, kam) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: balafons, ma'a drum. Festival(s): early January, formerly.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Éton (Edingding)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Éton (Edingding), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Éton (Edingding). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Éton (Edingding), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Éton (Edingding). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Cocoa is the main activity of the men; maize, groundnut, cassava, tomato and sesame are also grown. • Land belongs to the State unless there is a land title; seller and buyer go to the chief to pay the customary dues. • Ancestral forge work: crowbars, hoes, baskets, trays, drying racks and traditional beds.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Cocoa is the men's main activity; maize, groundnut, cassava, tomato and sesame are also grown. Land belongs to the State unless there is a land title; seller and buyer go to the chief to settle the customary dues.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Éton (Edingding)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Éton (Edingding)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death

vocabulary.langText: gibiers interdits aux enfants et femmes enceintes

lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Éton (Edingding), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Éton (Edingding). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Éton (Edingding), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Éton (Edingding). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • No ancestor cult. • Ngoag Ikula, “the bent rock”, at Minkama, is the place where unmarried men and women over 50 perform rites for the good of the group. • Birth is a reincarnation; death is natural. The dead are honoured at ceremonies, commemorations and prayers at graves. • Incest is forbidden; certain game animals are forbidden to children and pregnant women. • Desecrating a grave led to traditional imprisonment; to erase a serious offence, a live goat was split open.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: No ancestral cult. Ngoag Ikula, “the bent rock”, at Minkama, is the place where unmarried men and women over 50 perform rites for the good of the group.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Éton (Edingding) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Eton
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Éton (Edingding) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Éton (Edingding) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Éton (Edingding) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Éton (Edingding) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Eton. • Greeting formulae: Me koni = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Me ma kidi = morning greeting (one person); me ma kiri = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Po’og, Ba’a, La’, Na’a, Tan. • Each family has its ancestor: that of the Mvog-Andela is called Nkomo. • The group is renowned for its hospitality and solidarity, which bring it close to the Ewondo and the Bamiléké.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Eton are the first steps towards communicating with the Éton (Edingding). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.
